error_modes.label: Altitude control through the tactical turn

texts.0: SP, due to an uncompensated pitch input while the lead was tracked visually across the canopy, did not hold the briefed tactical altitude through the turn. Altitude diverged to about 1300 feet high on the reversal and about 700 feet low on the rollout, outside the +1000 / -500 feet limit. The IP took control to re-establish the assigned altitude before the next turn.
texts.1: SP, due to a late pitch correction while attention stayed on the lateral geometry, allowed altitude to reach the +1000 / -500 feet limit during the turn. The deviation persisted through most of the turn and was recovered only after the IP prompted verbally. No further excursion developed after the prompt.
texts.2: SP, due to an under-anticipated nose drop as bank was increased, drifted to about 800 feet above the briefed tactical altitude before checking the trend. The excursion stayed between the +500 / -300 and +1000 / -500 feet bands and was corrected in time without any input from the IP. Rollout was completed back on the assigned altitude.
texts.3: SP held the briefed tactical altitude within +500 / -300 feet through entry, turn and rollout. Pitch was compensated as bank was applied, so no altitude trend developed across successive turns. Energy was managed without trading altitude for position.
texts.4: SP flew the full sequence of tactical turns with altitude excursions of about 100 feet. Pitch compensation was applied with the bank input rather than after it, and every rollout arrived on the briefed altitude with no correction required.
texts.marginal: SP remained inside the +500 / -300 feet band, but finished each turn about 400 to 450 feet high, with the trend growing over successive turns. Corrections were reactive instead of being anticipated as bank increased. Improvement is expected toward a stable altitude that does not depend on late recovery.

texts_at.0: SP flew the tactical turn with IP calling the pitch compensation needed as bank was applied, due to this being one of the first tactical turn sequences SP has flown compensating pitch for bank through entry, turn and rollout. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to apply more of the pitch compensation independently on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP held the briefed tactical altitude through the turn, holding the deviation to no more than 500 feet low or 1000 feet high, at the outer edge of the standard, due to the pitch compensation for bank being applied only after the lead was reacquired visually rather than with the bank itself. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to apply pitch compensation with the bank itself, not after reacquiring lead visually.
texts_at.2: SP held the briefed tactical altitude through the turn, with the deviation at about 400 feet low and 700 feet high, due to the nose drop as bank increased being checked a beat after it began rather than as it began. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to check the nose drop as bank increases, not a beat after.
texts_at.3: SP held the briefed tactical altitude through the turn, holding the deviation to about 300 feet low and 500 feet high, due to energy being traded for position a fraction before pitch compensation was fully applied. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to fully apply pitch compensation before trading energy for position.

texts_above.1: SP held the briefed tactical altitude through the turn, holding the deviation to about +900 / -480 feet, at the edge of the standard. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP held the briefed tactical altitude through entry, turn and rollout, holding to about +700 / -400 feet, pitch compensated as bank was applied so no altitude trend developed across successive turns. Applying pitch compensation fully before trading energy for position would tighten the figure further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good pitch-compensation discipline.
texts_above.3: SP held the briefed tactical altitude to about +450 / -280 feet through the sequence, inside the code 3 tolerance, energy managed without trading altitude for position on any turn. The only refinement available was to hold that same compensation through the steepest reversal of the sequence. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good pitch-compensation discipline.
texts_above.4: SP flew the full sequence of tactical turns with altitude excursions of about 100 feet, pitch compensation applied with the bank input rather than after it, every rollout arriving on the briefed altitude with no correction required. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent pitch-compensation discipline.

texts.0: SP, due to power being left at the cruise setting while G was applied in the turn, did not maintain the briefed entry and exit airspeed. Speed decayed about 45 knots below the briefed value at the reversal and overshot about 40 knots on the rollout, outside the +/-30 knots limit. The IP took control of the throttle to restore the formation speed.
texts.1: SP, due to a delayed power addition as bank was increased, let the entry and exit airspeed reach the +/-30 knots limit. The speed was returned toward the briefed value only after repeated verbal prompting from the IP, and the recovery was slow enough that the next turn was entered off speed. No excursion beyond the limit occurred.
texts.2: SP, due to a power setting selected slightly late for the applied G, allowed entry speed to fall about 22 knots below the briefed value. The deviation stayed between the +/-15 and +/-30 knots bands and was recognized and corrected before the rollout without IP input. Exit speed was re-established for the following turn.
texts.3: SP maintained entry and exit airspeed within +/-15 knots of the briefed value throughout the tactical turns. Power was led against the G application so that speed was stable at each rollout. Corrections were small and applied without overshoot.
texts.4: SP held entry and exit airspeed within about 5 knots of the briefed value for every turn. Throttle was moved in anticipation of the G loading rather than in response to a speed trend, so no speed correction was needed after rollout.
texts.marginal: SP stayed within the +/-15 knots band, but was consistently 12 to 14 knots slow at the exit of each turn, and the shortfall increased through the sequence. Power was added after the speed trend appeared rather than with the bank input. Improvement is expected toward speed control that does not require catching up on the following leg.

texts_at.0: SP flew the tactical turn entry and exit with IP calling the power needed to lead the applied G, due to this being one of the first tactical turn sequences SP has flown leading power against G rather than reacting to a speed trend. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to lead more of the power independently against the applied G on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP maintained the briefed entry and exit airspeed, holding the deviation to about 30 knots, at the edge of the standard, due to the power addition following the applied G by a beat rather than being led against it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to lead the power addition against the applied G, not follow it by a beat.
texts_at.2: SP maintained the briefed entry and exit airspeed, holding the deviation to about 21 knots, due to the power setting being selected a beat after the G was applied rather than with it. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to select the power setting with the applied G, not a beat after.
texts_at.3: SP maintained the briefed entry and exit airspeed, holding the deviation to about 15 knots, due to exit speed being confirmed a fraction after the rollout rather than through it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to confirm exit speed through the rollout, not a fraction after.

texts_above.1: SP maintained the briefed entry and exit airspeed, holding the deviation to about 27 knots, at the edge of the standard. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP maintained entry and exit airspeed throughout the tactical turns, holding to about 21 knots, power led against the G application so speed was stable at each rollout. Confirming exit speed through the rollout itself, rather than a fraction after, would tighten the figure further. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sound power-lead discipline.
texts_above.3: SP maintained entry and exit airspeed to about 13 knots on every turn, corrections small and applied without overshoot throughout the sequence. The only refinement available was to hold that same lead through the fastest turn of the sequence. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to sure-handed power-lead discipline.
texts_above.4: SP held entry and exit airspeed within about 5 knots of the briefed value for every turn, throttle moved in anticipation of the G loading rather than in response to a speed trend so no speed correction was needed after rollout. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exceptional power-lead discipline.

texts.0: SP, due to rate of turn not being assessed against the required heading change, did not roll out on the briefed recovery heading. The rollout was about 45 degrees past the required heading on the delay turn and required a reversal to regain the formation axis, outside the +/-30 degrees limit. The IP took control to recover the briefed course.
texts.1: SP, due to a late start of the rollout on the tactical turn, arrived on a recovery heading at the +/-30 degrees limit. The heading was corrected only after the IP called the error, and the correction took the whole following leg. No further overshoot occurred after the call.
texts.2: SP, due to a rollout rate that did not match the applied bank, passed the briefed recovery heading by about 20 degrees. The error stayed between the +/-10 and +/-30 degrees bands and was recognized and corrected promptly without IP input. The formation axis was re-established before the next turn was called.
texts.3: SP rolled out within +/-10 degrees of the briefed recovery heading on each tactical turn. The rollout was started at a point consistent with the turn rate, so no reversal was needed afterwards. Heading was then held steady through the following leg.
texts.4: SP arrived on the briefed recovery heading within about 3 degrees on every turn of the sequence. The rollout point was anticipated from the turn rate, and no heading correction was required after wings level.
texts.marginal: SP stayed within the +/-10 degrees band, but rolled out 8 to 9 degrees past the briefed heading on each turn, always in the same direction. The rollout was started slightly late and the error was absorbed on the following leg. Improvement is expected toward a rollout point that removes the repeated overshoot.

texts_at.0: SP rolled out of the tactical turn with IP calling the rate of turn needed against the required heading change, due to this being one of the first tactical turn sequences SP has flown assessing the rate of turn against a required heading change before rollout. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to assess more of the rate of turn independently before rollout on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP rolled out on the briefed recovery heading, holding the error to about 30 degrees, at the edge of the standard, due to the rate of turn being assessed against the required heading change only as the rollout began rather than before it. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to assess the rate of turn against the required change before the rollout begins.
texts_at.2: SP rolled out on the briefed recovery heading, holding the error to about 18 degrees, due to the rollout rate being matched to the applied bank a beat late rather than from the start of the rollout. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to match the rollout rate to the applied bank from the start, not a beat late.
texts_at.3: SP rolled out on the briefed recovery heading, holding the error to about 10 degrees, due to the rollout being started a fraction later than the rate of turn called for. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to start the rollout exactly when the rate of turn calls for it.

texts_above.1: SP rolled out on the briefed recovery heading, holding the error to about 27 degrees, at the edge of the standard. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP rolled out on the briefed recovery heading on each tactical turn, holding to about 18 degrees, the rollout started at a point consistent with the turn rate so no reversal was needed afterwards. Starting the rollout exactly when the rate of turn calls for it, rather than a fraction later, would remove the repeated overshoot. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to solid rollout-timing discipline.
texts_above.3: SP rolled out to about 9 degrees of the briefed recovery heading on each turn, heading then held steady through the following leg. The only refinement available was to hold that same timing through the sharpest turn of the sequence. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to well-developed rollout-timing discipline.
texts_above.4: SP arrived on the briefed recovery heading within about 3 degrees on every turn of the sequence, the rollout point anticipated from the turn rate with no heading correction required after wings level. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to outstanding rollout-timing discipline.

error_modes.label: Continuous G control during the turn

texts.0: SP, due to stick inputs made in steps while the lead was reacquired visually, did not sustain the briefed continuous G through the turn. Loading varied by about 1.5 G either side of the briefed value, outside the +/-1.0 G limit, and the resulting geometry could not be flown back to position. The IP took control to stabilize the turn.
texts.1: SP, due to G being relaxed each time the lead moved in the canopy, allowed the loading to reach the +/-1.0 G limit during the turn. The briefed G was re-established only after the IP prompted verbally, and the variation continued through the first part of the turn. No excursion beyond the limit occurred.
texts.2: SP, due to an uneven pull as bank was set, varied the continuous G by about 0.8 G from the briefed value. The variation stayed between the +/-0.5 and +/-1.0 G bands and was smoothed out during the same turn without IP input. The turn was completed with the briefed loading.
texts.3: SP sustained the briefed continuous G within +/-0,5 G through each tactical turn. Stick inputs were smooth and the loading was set with the bank rather than adjusted after it. Energy was converted as briefed without unloading in the middle of the turn.
texts.4: SP flew the tactical turns with continuous G held within about 0,2 G of the briefed value. Loading was applied smoothly at entry and released only at the rollout, so the turn geometry stayed exactly as planned.
texts.marginal: SP kept the loading inside the +/-0,5 G band, but the G trace varied by 0,4 G within each turn, with a relaxation every time attention moved to the lead. The turn was completed as briefed, but the geometry had to be corrected on the following leg. Improvement is expected toward a steady pull that does not vary with visual acquisition of the lead.

texts_at.0: SP flew the tactical turn with IP calling the loading to set with the bank and hold through the reversal, due to this being one of the first tactical turn sequences SP has flown setting continuous G with the bank rather than adjusting it afterward. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to set more of the loading independently with the bank on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP sustained the briefed continuous G through the turn, holding the variation to no more than 1.0 G, at the outer edge of the standard, due to the G being relaxed each time the lead was reacquired visually rather than held through the reacquisition. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to hold the G through every visual reacquisition of the lead, not relax it.
texts_at.2: SP sustained the briefed continuous G through the turn, holding the loading excursion to about 0.75 G, due to the pull being uneven as bank was set rather than smoothed into a single input. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to smooth the pull into a single input as bank is set.
texts_at.3: SP sustained the briefed continuous G through the turn, holding the variation inside 0.5 G, due to the loading settling a fraction after bank was established rather than with it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to settle the loading with bank as it is established, not a fraction after.

texts_above.1: SP sustained the briefed continuous G through the turn, holding the variation to about 0.88 G, at the edge of the standard. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP sustained the briefed continuous G through each tactical turn, holding to about 0.65 G, stick inputs smooth with the loading set with the bank rather than adjusted after it. Settling the loading with bank as it is established, rather than a fraction after, would tighten the figure further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady G-smoothness discipline.
texts_above.3: SP sustained continuous G to about 0.4 G through the sequence, energy converted as briefed without unloading in the middle of any turn. The only refinement available was to hold that same smooth pull through the longest turn of the sequence. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate G-smoothness discipline.
texts_above.4: SP flew the tactical turns with continuous G held within about 0.2 G of the briefed value, loading applied smoothly at entry and released only at the rollout so the turn geometry stayed exactly as planned. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary G-smoothness discipline.

error_modes.label: Line abreast position after the turn

texts.0: SP, due to the turn being started without assessing the lead's relative position, did not roll out in the tactical formation position. The aircraft settled about 45 degrees aft of the line abreast reference, outside the +/-30 degrees limit, and the position could not be regained with the available energy. The IP took control and repositioned the aircraft.
texts.1: SP, due to a turn started late relative to the lead, rolled out at the +/-30 degrees limit from the line abreast reference. The position was closed up only after the IP prompted verbally, and the correction was still running when the next turn was called. No deviation beyond the limit developed.
texts.2: SP, due to a rate of turn that did not match the lead's, rolled out about 20 degrees aft of the line abreast reference. The deviation stayed between the +/-10 and +/-30 degrees bands and was corrected with a timely energy adjustment without IP input. The line abreast position was regained before the next turn.
texts.3: SP rolled out within +/-10 degrees of the line abreast reference on each tactical turn. The turn was started at the correct point relative to the lead and the aircraft energy was converted to hold the position. No repositioning was needed on the following leg.
texts.4: SP maintained the line abreast position within about 5 degrees on every turn of the sequence. The correction technique was applied continuously through the turn, so the formation position never had to be regained after rollout.
texts.marginal: SP stayed within the +/-10 degrees band, but rolled out 8 to 9 degrees aft of the line abreast reference on each turn and closed the gap on the following leg. The correction was applied after the rollout rather than inside the turn. Improvement is expected toward holding the position through the turn instead of regaining it afterwards.

texts_at.0: SP rolled out toward the line abreast position with IP calling the lead's relative position to assess before the turn starts, due to this being one of the first tactical turn sequences SP has flown assessing the lead's position before turning to regain line abreast. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to assess more of the lead's relative position independently before the turn on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP rolled out in the tactical formation position, holding the deviation from line abreast to about 30 degrees, at the edge of the standard, due to the lead's relative position being assessed only as the turn started rather than before it. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to assess the lead's relative position before the turn starts, not as it starts.
texts_at.2: SP rolled out in the tactical formation position, holding the deviation from line abreast to about 18 degrees, due to the rate of turn being matched to the lead's a beat late rather than from the entry. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to match the rate of turn to the lead's from the entry, not a beat late.
texts_at.3: SP rolled out in the tactical formation position, holding the deviation from line abreast to about 10 degrees, due to the energy adjustment closing the gap a fraction after the rollout rather than through the turn itself. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to close the gap through the turn itself, not a fraction after the rollout.

texts_above.1: SP rolled out in the tactical formation position, holding the deviation from line abreast to about 27 degrees, at the edge of the standard. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP rolled out toward the line abreast reference on each tactical turn, holding to about 18 degrees, the turn started at the correct point relative to the lead with aircraft energy converted to hold the position. Closing the gap through the turn itself, rather than a fraction after the rollout, would remove the need to regain it afterward. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to dependable in-turn-correction discipline.
texts_above.3: SP rolled out to about 9 degrees of the line abreast reference on each turn, no repositioning needed on the following leg. The only refinement available was to hold that same in-turn correction through the sharpest reversal of the sequence. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to notably good in-turn-correction discipline.
texts_above.4: SP maintained the line abreast position within about 5 degrees on every turn of the sequence, the correction technique applied continuously through the turn so the formation position never had to be regained after rollout. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to superior in-turn-correction discipline.

texts.0: SP, due to the briefed spread not being re-established after the reversal, did not maintain the required lateral separation. The distance opened to about 2500 feet more than briefed on one turn and closed inside the safe spread on the next, outside the +/- 1000 feet limit. The IP took control to restore separation.
texts.1: SP, due to a delayed adjustment of the turn geometry, allowed lateral separation to reach the +/- 1000 feet limit after the rollout. The spread was corrected only after the IP prompted verbally, and the aircraft flew the following leg while still closing. No excursion beyond the limit occurred.
texts.2: SP, due to a rollout heading slightly divergent from the lead's, allowed lateral separation to open by about 750 feet from the briefed spread. The deviation stayed between the +/- 500 and +/- 1000 feet bands and was recognized and corrected without IP input. Separation was back inside the briefed spread before the next turn.
texts.3: SP maintained lateral separation within +/- 500 feet of the briefed spread through the tactical turns. The turn geometry was flown so that the spread was preserved at rollout rather than rebuilt afterwards. Separation stayed safe and workable for the next turn at all times.
texts.4: SP held lateral separation within about 150 feet of the briefed spread throughout the sequence. Each rollout placed the aircraft at the planned distance from the lead, with no closing or opening trend on any leg.
texts.marginal: SP remained inside the +/- 500 feet band, but the spread opened by 400 to 450 feet after every turn and had to be closed on the following leg. The correction was applied after separation had already grown rather than during the turn. Improvement is expected toward a turn geometry that preserves the briefed spread at rollout.

texts_at.0: SP flew the tactical turn with IP calling when to preserve the briefed spread through the reversal, due to this being one of the first tactical turn sequences SP has flown preserving lateral spread through a reversal rather than rebuilding it after. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to preserve more of the briefed spread independently through the reversal on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP maintained the required lateral separation, holding the deviation to about 1000 feet, at the edge of the standard, due to the briefed spread being re-established only after the reversal rather than preserved through it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to preserve the briefed spread through the reversal, not re-establish it after.
texts_at.2: SP maintained the required lateral separation, holding the deviation to about 680 feet, due to the turn geometry being adjusted a beat after the rollout rather than through the turn. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to adjust the turn geometry through the turn itself, not a beat after rollout.
texts_at.3: SP maintained the required lateral separation, holding the deviation to about 500 feet, due to the rollout heading diverging a fraction from the lead's before it was corrected. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to hold the rollout heading matched to the lead's from the first degree of divergence.

texts_above.1: SP maintained the required lateral separation, holding the deviation to about 900 feet, at the edge of the standard. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP maintained lateral separation toward the briefed spread through the tactical turns, holding to about 680 feet, the turn geometry flown so the spread was preserved at rollout rather than rebuilt afterwards. Holding the rollout heading matched to the lead's from the first degree of divergence would tighten the figure further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to assured spread-preservation discipline.
texts_above.3: SP maintained lateral separation to about 400 feet of the briefed spread through the sequence, separation staying safe and workable for the next turn at all times. The only refinement available was to hold that same match through the fastest reversal of the sequence. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to precise spread-preservation discipline.
texts_above.4: SP held lateral separation within about 150 feet of the briefed spread throughout the sequence, each rollout placing the aircraft at the planned distance from the lead with no closing or opening trend on any leg. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to first-rate spread-preservation discipline.

error_modes.label: Clearing of the responsibility airspace and terrain awareness

texts.0: SP, due to loss of situational awareness of the aircraft's position relative to the terrain and the flight, did not check the corresponding responsibility airspace during the turn and did not ensure safe altitude for maneuvering over mountains. The turn was flown with the scan fixed on the lead and with the ridge line inside the turn radius, and the flight path went below the briefed terrain clearance. The IP took control and repositioned the aircraft away from the high ground.
texts.1: SP, due to degraded situational awareness after the direction of turn was changed, cleared only the sector the lead occupied and left the assigned responsibility airspace unchecked. Clearing and terrain assessment were carried out only after repeated verbal direction from the IP, and the delay left the turn established before the sector was cleared. Safe altitude over the terrain was never actually lost.
texts.2: SP, due to situational awareness limited to the lead's position at the start of the turn, began the reversal before completing the clearing of the responsibility airspace. The omission was recognized within the first part of the turn and the sector and terrain clearance were checked in time without IP input. The remaining turns were entered with the airspace cleared.
texts.3: SP checked the corresponding responsibility airspace before and during each turn and confirmed safe altitude for maneuvering over the terrain. Clearing was carried out without losing the lead's position, and the assessment covered the sector into which the flight was turning. No prompting was required at any point.
texts.4: SP cleared the assigned responsibility airspace continuously through the sequence and kept terrain clearance assessed ahead of each turn. Traffic and high ground in the turn sector were identified and called before the turn was initiated, with the lead kept in sight throughout.
texts.marginal: SP cleared the responsibility airspace and maintained safe terrain clearance, but the sweep of the sector was brief and was completed just as the turn was being initiated. Terrain was assessed once at the start rather than reassessed as the flight moved over the ridge. Improvement is expected toward clearing that is completed before turn entry and updated during the turn.

texts_at.0: SP cleared the responsibility airspace with IP calling the sector sweep to complete and the terrain to reassess through the turn, due to this being one of the first tactical turn sequences SP has flown clearing a sector and reassessing terrain through a reversal. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to complete more of the sector sweep independently before the turn on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP checked the corresponding responsibility airspace before the turn, due to the sector sweep being brief and completed only as the turn was initiated rather than before it. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to complete the sector sweep before the turn is initiated, not as it begins.
texts_at.2: SP checked the corresponding responsibility airspace before the turn, due to terrain being assessed once at the start rather than reassessed as the flight moved over the ridge. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to reassess terrain as the flight moves over the ridge, not only once at the start.
texts_at.3: SP checked the corresponding responsibility airspace before the turn, due to the sector and terrain clearance being checked a fraction after the reversal began rather than through it. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to check sector and terrain clearance through the reversal itself, not a fraction after it begins.

texts_above.1: SP checked the corresponding responsibility airspace before the turn. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP checked the corresponding responsibility airspace before and during each turn and confirmed safe altitude for maneuvering over the terrain, clearing carried out without losing the lead's position with the assessment covering the sector into which the flight was turning. Checking sector and terrain clearance through the reversal itself, rather than a fraction after it begins, would complete the clearing discipline. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent terrain-clearance discipline.
texts_above.3: SP checked the corresponding responsibility airspace before every turn, no prompting required at any point of the sequence. The only refinement available was to reassess terrain a second time through the longest turn of the sequence. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined terrain-clearance discipline.
texts_above.4: SP cleared the assigned responsibility airspace continuously through the sequence and kept terrain clearance assessed ahead of each turn, traffic and high ground in the turn sector identified and called before the turn was initiated with the lead kept in sight throughout. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to faultless terrain-clearance discipline.

error_modes.label: Energy exploitation and correction technique to regain tactical position

texts.0: SP, due to bank and power being used without any plan for the aircraft energy, did not exploit and convert the energy in order to maintain the tactical position. Airspeed was allowed to bleed in the turn and then recovered with full power on the leg, so the correction technique for returning to tactical formation position was never established and fuel was consumed well beyond the briefed reserve planning. The IP took control to restore the formation geometry.
texts.1: SP, due to a correction attempted only with power instead of turn geometry, did not convert the aircraft energy to hold the tactical position. The technique was applied correctly only after the IP described it verbally, and the position was regained late enough that the following turn was entered out of position. Fuel state remained inside the briefed reserve.
texts.2: SP, due to an early power reduction that removed the energy needed for the correction, drifted out of the tactical position after the rollout. The correction technique was then applied in time, converting turn geometry rather than power alone, and the position was regained without IP input. Engine handling stayed consistent with the briefed fuel reserve.
texts.3: SP exploited and converted the aircraft energy to hold the tactical formation position through the turns. The correction technique was applied with turn geometry first and power as a supplement, so the position was maintained rather than rebuilt. Engine handling remained consistent with the briefed fuel reserve.
texts.4: SP managed the aircraft energy so that the tactical position was preserved through every turn without any large correction being needed. Power changes were small and anticipatory, the correction technique was applied continuously, and fuel consumption stayed well within the planned reserve.
texts.marginal: SP maintained the tactical position and stayed inside the briefed fuel reserve, but the corrections relied mainly on power, with several excursions to a high power setting on each leg. Turn geometry was used only after the power correction proved insufficient. Improvement is expected toward energy conversion as the primary correction technique.

texts_at.0: SP corrected the tactical position with IP calling when to bring in turn geometry alongside power, due to this being one of the first tactical turn sequences SP has flown converting energy with geometry rather than power alone. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to bring in more of the turn geometry independently on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP exploited and converted the aircraft energy to hold the tactical position, holding the line abreast deviation to no more than 30 degrees, at the outer edge of the standard, due to one correction relying on power alone before turn geometry was brought in as well. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to bring in turn geometry from the first correction, not power alone.
texts_at.2: SP exploited and converted the aircraft energy to hold the tactical position, holding the line abreast error to about 20 degrees, due to the correction technique being applied a beat after the drift was noticed rather than as it was noticed. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to apply the correction technique as the drift is noticed, not a beat after.
texts_at.3: SP exploited and converted the aircraft energy to hold the tactical position, holding the line abreast deviation to about 10 degrees, due to engine handling being confirmed against the fuel reserve a fraction after the correction rather than with it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to confirm engine handling against the fuel reserve with the correction, not a fraction after.

texts_above.1: SP exploited and converted the aircraft energy to hold the tactical position. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP exploited and converted the aircraft energy to hold the tactical formation position through the turns, the correction technique applied with turn geometry first and power as a supplement so the position was maintained rather than rebuilt. Confirming engine handling against the fuel reserve with the correction, rather than a fraction after, would trim the power usage further. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to good energy-conversion discipline.
texts_above.3: SP exploited and converted the aircraft energy to hold the tactical position through the sequence, engine handling remaining consistent with the briefed fuel reserve throughout. The only refinement available was to bring in turn geometry a moment earlier still on the fastest correction. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to very good energy-conversion discipline.
texts_above.4: SP managed the aircraft energy so the tactical position was preserved through every turn without any large correction being needed, power changes small and anticipatory, the correction technique applied continuously with fuel consumption staying well within the planned reserve. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to excellent energy-conversion discipline.

error_modes.label: Comm-out visual signals and turn communication

texts.0: SP, due to failure to pass the required call at the briefed point, did not execute the visual signals for the comm-out turn as described in the Techniques and Procedures Manual. The signal was neither given as leader nor acknowledged as wingman, the turn was started with the flight unsynchronized, and the two aircraft turned in opposite directions. The IP took control and re-established the flight integrity.
texts.1: SP, due to an indirect indication instead of the briefed visual signal, left the intention of the turn ambiguous to the other aircraft. The correct signal was given only after the IP directed it verbally, and the turn was delayed until the flight was synchronized. The turn was then executed as described in the manual.
texts.2: SP, due to a visual signal given late and with limited amplitude for the range, was not immediately understood by the other aircraft. The signal was recognized as inadequate and repeated correctly before the turn was initiated, without IP input. The remaining comm-out turns were signalled and acknowledged at the correct points.
texts.3: SP knew and executed the visual signals for the comm-out turns and acknowledged the signals received as briefed. Each turn was initiated only after the flight was synchronized, and the maneuver was flown as described in the Techniques and Procedures Manual. No verbal backup was required.
texts.4: SP gave and acknowledged every comm-out visual signal clearly and at the correct point in the sequence. The signals were sized for the actual range, each turn was initiated with the flight fully synchronized, and the execution matched the Techniques and Procedures Manual throughout.
texts.marginal: SP executed the comm-out visual signals correctly, but they were given close to the turn point, leaving the other aircraft little time to acknowledge before the turn started. Acknowledgements were confirmed only once, without a check that the signal had been read. Improvement is expected toward signals given early enough to confirm synchronization before the turn.

texts_at.0: SP signalled the comm-out turn with IP calling when to give the signal early enough to confirm synchronization, due to this being one of the first comm-out tactical turns SP has flown signalling and confirming synchronization before turning. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to give more of the signal independently early enough to confirm synchronization on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP knew and executed the visual signals for the comm-out turns, due to the signal being given close to the turn point rather than early enough to confirm synchronization. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to give the signal early enough to confirm synchronization, not close to the turn point.
texts_at.2: SP knew and executed the visual signals for the comm-out turns, due to the acknowledgement being confirmed only once rather than checked a second time. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to check the acknowledgement a second time, not confirm it only once.
texts_at.3: SP knew and executed the visual signals for the comm-out turns, due to the turn being initiated a fraction after full synchronization was confirmed rather than exactly at it. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to initiate the turn exactly at full synchronization, not a fraction after.

texts_above.1: SP knew and executed the visual signals for the comm-out turns. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP knew and executed the visual signals for the comm-out turns and acknowledged the signals received as briefed, each turn initiated only after the flight was synchronized with the maneuver flown as described in the Techniques and Procedures Manual. Initiating the turn exactly at full synchronization, rather than a fraction after, would sharpen the timing further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to sound signal-timing discipline.
texts_above.3: SP knew and executed the visual signals for the comm-out turns, no verbal backup required at any point of the sequence. The only refinement available was to give the signal a beat earlier still on the fastest-developing turn. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sure-handed signal-timing discipline.
texts_above.4: SP gave and acknowledged every comm-out visual signal clearly and at the correct point in the sequence, the signals sized for the actual range with each turn initiated with the flight fully synchronized and execution matching the Techniques and Procedures Manual throughout. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to exceptional signal-timing discipline.

error_modes.label: Initiative for safe separation during the turns

texts.0: SP, due to lack of assertiveness in voicing a recognized unsafe condition, did not take the initiative for safe separation during the tactical turns. The closure with the other aircraft was seen and not called, the turn was continued as briefed, and the flight paths converged inside the briefed spread. The IP took control and called a knock-it-off to separate the aircraft.
texts.1: SP, due to hesitation to state that the geometry was no longer workable, delayed taking the initiative for safe separation after the reversal. The corrective turn and the call were made only after the IP directed them, and the separation had already reduced to the minimum briefed value. Separation was then re-established without further closure.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial reluctance to break the briefed sequence, was slow to react to the converging geometry after the turn. The condition was then called and the turn adjusted in time, restoring safe separation without IP input. The remaining turns were flown with separation assessed before each entry.
texts.3: SP took the initiative for safe separation during the tactical turns and adjusted the geometry whenever the closure rate required it. The condition was stated clearly to the other aircraft, and each turn was executed as described in the Techniques and Procedures Manual with the rollout in tactical formation position. No IP direction was needed.
texts.4: SP anticipated the closure geometry ahead of each turn and acted for safe separation before the situation developed. The intentions were stated clearly and early, the adjustments were small, and every turn was completed as described in the Techniques and Procedures Manual with the rollout in tactical formation position.
texts.marginal: SP maintained safe separation throughout, but the initiative was taken only once the closure had become obvious, and the calls were made with a questioning rather than a directive tone. The turns were still completed as briefed and separation was never at risk. Improvement is expected toward earlier recognition and a clear statement of the required action.

texts_at.0: SP flew the tactical turn with IP calling when to state the closure call for safe separation, due to this being one of the first tactical turn sequences SP has flown stating a closure call for safe separation. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to state more of the closure call independently at its first indication on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP took the initiative for safe separation during the tactical turns, holding the lateral separation to no more than 1000 feet from the briefed spacing, at the outer edge of the standard, due to the closure being called only once it had become obvious rather than at its first indication. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to call the closure at its first indication, not once it has become obvious.
texts_at.2: SP took the initiative for safe separation during the tactical turns, with the lateral separation off the briefed spacing by about 700 feet, due to the call being phrased as a question rather than a directive statement. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to phrase the call as a directive statement, not a question.
texts_at.3: SP took the initiative for safe separation during the tactical turns, holding the lateral separation to 500 feet of the briefed spacing, due to the geometry being adjusted a fraction after the call rather than with it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to adjust the geometry with the call itself, not a fraction after.

texts_above.1: SP took the initiative for safe separation during the tactical turns. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP took the initiative for safe separation during the tactical turns and adjusted the geometry whenever the closure rate required it, the condition stated clearly to the other aircraft with each turn executed as described in the Techniques and Procedures Manual. Adjusting the geometry with the call itself, rather than a fraction after, would sharpen the initiative further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid closure-anticipation discipline.
texts_above.3: SP took the initiative for safe separation during the tactical turns, no IP direction needed at any point of the sequence. The only refinement available was to call the closure a moment earlier still on the fastest-developing turn. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed closure-anticipation discipline.
texts_above.4: SP anticipated the closure geometry ahead of each turn and acted for safe separation before the situation developed, the intentions stated clearly and early with the adjustments small and every turn completed as described in the Techniques and Procedures Manual with the rollout in tactical formation position. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding closure-anticipation discipline.
